q-86533.name: Question 1
q-86533.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})^{2}$ at the point $A(-1,-1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(2,0).$
q-86533.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨2,0⟩-⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨3,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨3,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨8x(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}),\,36{y}^{3}-24{x}^{2}y⟩ \\ ∇f(-1,-1) & =⟨8(-1)\cdot (2(-1)^{2}-3(-1)^{2}),36(-1)^{3}-24(-1)^{2}(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨8,-12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,-1) & =∇f(-1,-1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨8,-12⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟩ \\  & =8\cdot \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}-12\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{6\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The directional derivative fu′(a,b) of a function f(x,y) at the point (a,b) in the direction of the vector v is given by

fu′(a,b)=∇f(a,b)⋅u

where u is a unit vector in the direction of v.

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

AB→=⟨2,0⟩−⟨−1,−1⟩=⟨3,1⟩u=AB→‖AB→‖=132+12⟨3,1⟩=110⟨3,1⟩

Now, we calculate the gradient ∇f(x,y) and evaluate it at the point A(−1,−1):

∇f(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(2x2−3y2)2,∂∂y(2x2−3y2)2⟩=⟨8x(2x2−3y2),36y3−24x2y⟩∇f(−1,−1)=⟨8(−1)⋅(2(−1)2−3(−1)2),36(−1)3−24(−1)2(−1)⟩=⟨8,−12⟩

Therefore, the directional derivative is

fu′(−1,−1)=∇f(−1,−1)⋅u=⟨8,−12⟩⋅⟨310,110⟩=8⋅310−12⋅110=1210=6105.

q-130257.name: Question 2
q-130257.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ at the point $(2,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=\sqrt{3}\,i+j.$
q-130257.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=2 \\ u & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\,i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)\text{ }j \\  & =y\,i+x\,j \\ ∇\,f(2,1) & =i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(2,1) & =∇\,f(2,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+2\,j)\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\,i+j) \\  & =\frac{1(\sqrt{3})+2(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}+2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-36306.name: Question 3
q-36306.problem:
Given the function  $g(x,y)=({x}^{2}+y)^{2}$, find its directional derivative at the
point $A(-1,1)$ in the direction that's towards the point $B(3,4).$
q-36306.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨3,4⟩-⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,3⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}}⟨4,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨4,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y)^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨4x({x}^{2}+y),\,2({x}^{2}+y)⟩ \\ ∇g(-1,1) & =⟨4\cdot (-1)\cdot ((-1)^{2}+1),2\cdot ((-1)^{2}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇g(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-8,4⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}⟩ \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{4}{5}+4\cdot \frac{3}{5} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-86429.name: Question 4
q-86429.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=6{x}^{2}+2y$ at the point $(0,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=3i+5j.$
q-86429.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}}=\sqrt{34} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{34}}(3i+5j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}+2y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}+2y)\text{ }j \\  & =12x\,i+2\,j \\ ∇\,f(0,1) & =(12\cdot 0)\,i+2\,j \\  & =2j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(0,1) & =∇\,f(0,1)\cdot u \\  & =2j\cdot (\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}i+\frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}j) \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 3+2\cdot 5}{\sqrt{34}} \\  & =\frac{10\sqrt{34}}{34}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130263.name: Question 5
q-130263.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=i-j.$
q-130263.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(2(1)-1)\,i+(2(1)-1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j) \\  & =\frac{1(1)+1(-1)}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

In what direction does the function g(x,y,z)=4z2+2ln⁡(x−y) increase most rapidly at the point (2,−1,0)?

a
⟨23,−23,2⟩
b
⟨32,−23,2⟩
c
⟨23,−23,0⟩
d
⟨32,32,0⟩
e
−⟨23,23,0⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function g(x,y,z) increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute ∇g(x,y,z) and evaluate it at the point (2,−1,0):

∇g(x,y,z)=⟨∂∂x(4z2+2ln⁡(x−y)),∂∂y(4z2+2ln⁡(x−y)),∂∂z(4z2+2ln⁡(x−y))⟩=⟨2x−y,−2x−y,8z⟩∇g(2,−1,0)=⟨22−(−1),−22−(−1),8⋅0⟩=⟨23,−23,0⟩

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of ⟨23,−23,0⟩.

q-83598.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,1,1)?$
q-83598.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇g(x,y,z) & =-⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z))⟩ \\  & =-⟨{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{x+z},\,2xy,\,-\frac{4}{x+z}⟩ \\ -∇g(1,1,1) & =-⟨{1}^{2}-\frac{4}{1+1},\,2\cdot 1\cdot 1,\,-\frac{4}{1+1}⟩ \\  & =-⟨-1,\,2,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨1,\,-2,\,2⟩.$

q-83598.html:
Question 7
?

In what direction does the function g(x,y,z)=xy2−4ln⁡(x+z) decrease most rapidly at the point (1,1,1)?

a
 ⟨0,−2,1⟩
b
 ⟨3,4,−4⟩
c
 ⟨−1,2,−2⟩
d
 ⟨−3,−4,4⟩
e
 ⟨1,−2,2⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function g(x,y,z) decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute −∇g(x,y,z) and evaluate it at the point (1,1,1):

−∇g(x,y,z)=−⟨∂∂x(xy2+4ln⁡(x+z)),∂∂y(xy2+4ln⁡(x+z)),∂∂z(xy2+4ln⁡(x+z))⟩=−⟨y2−4x+z,2xy,−4x+z⟩−∇g(1,1,1)=−⟨12−41+1,2⋅1⋅1,−41+1⟩=−⟨−1,2,−2⟩=⟨1,−2,2⟩

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of ⟨1,−2,2⟩.

q-130272.name: Question 8
q-130272.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)=x{z}^{2}-{y}^{3}$ increase most rapidly at the point $(0,1,2)?$
q-130272.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{2}-{y}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{z}^{2}-{y}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{2}-{y}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨{z}^{2},\,-3{y}^{2},\,2xz⟩ \\ ∇g(0,1,2) & =⟨{2}^{2},-3(1)^{2},2(0)(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨4,-3,0⟩.$

q-86537.problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ increase most rapidly at the point $(0,1)?$
q-86537.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =(y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+6x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\text{ }i+(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+6\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\text{ }i+(3(0)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))\text{ }j \\  & =-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $-j.$

q-86542.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨2,4⟩?$
q-86542.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}⟨2,4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{y}}{{x}^{2}y},\,\frac{{e}^{y}(y-1)}{x{y}^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,1) & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{1}}{{1}^{2}\cdot 1},\,\frac{{e}^{1}\cdot (1-1)}{1\cdot {1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇g(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-e\cdot 1+0\cdot 2) \\  & =-\frac{e}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\frac{e\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The rate of change of g(x,y) at the point (1,1) in the direction of v is equal to the directional derivative gu′(1,1).

First, we find the unit vector u in the direction of v:

‖v‖=22+42=20=25u=125⟨2,4⟩=15⟨1,2⟩

Now, we find the gradient ∇g(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (1,1):

∇g(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(eyyx),∂∂y(eyyx)⟩=⟨−eyx2y,ey(y−1)xy2⟩∇g(1,1)=⟨−e112⋅1,e1⋅(1−1)1⋅12⟩=⟨−e,0⟩

Finally, the directional derivative gu′(1,1) is
